result.summary: The Messenians and Lacedaemonians clash in a fierce pitched battle. Euphaes and Theopompus meet and rout each other's opponents on one wing, but the fight ends indecisively at nightfall. Next day both sides bury their dead by agreement.

scenes.title: The armies clash
scenes.summary: Both armies charge, trade insults and fight hard. The Lacedaemonians have experience and numbers, while the Messenians fight with despair and mutual encouragement.
scenes.stakes: The Messenians risk death and enslavement; the Lacedaemonians risk failing to subdue Messenia.

scenes.title: Kings fight; night ends it
scenes.summary: Euphaes and Theopompus meet, and Euphaes' picked guard routs Theopompus. The other Messenian wing collapses after Pytharatus dies, and darkness stops the battle in a draw.
scenes.stakes: Euphaes risks death in single combat and the loss of his army's cohesion.

scenes.title: Truce to bury the dead
scenes.summary: Neither side renews battle or sets up a trophy; heralds agree on burying the dead.

notable_quotes.reason: Euphaes compares Theopompus to Polynices, invoking the Theban curse of kin-slaying.

analysis.text: The battle contrasts Spartan discipline with Messenian desperate courage, and both sides see the war as a kin conflict among Dorians.
The passage reflects archaic hoplite warfare, with a deep phalanx, weak cavalry, and a Spartan custom of not pursuing broken enemies.

fun_facts.text: Pausanias wrote in the 2nd century AD, centuries after the First Messenian War, relying on earlier sources such as Rhianus and Myron.

language_notes.text: "At the double" means at a running pace; the Messenians charge rather than march.
The Messenians call the Spartans kinsmen because both claimed descent from the Dorians and from Hercules' line; attacking kin was thus impious.
Helots were the Spartans' state-owned serfs, mostly from conquered Messenia; calling the Messenians no freer than Helots is a deep insult.
"Suppliants" are people who seek protection by humbly begging, a status religion required hosts to respect.
"No quarter was asked for" means neither side begged for mercy or expected it.
Polynices led an Argive army against Thebes, his native city, and he and his brother Eteocles killed each other. Euphaes compares Theopompus to him.
"Peloponnesians" are inhabitants of the Peloponnese, the southern Greek peninsula including Laconia and Messenia.

context_notes.text: Spartan discipline prized keeping a tight formation (the phalanx) over individual daring.
Cretan archers were famous mercenaries in Greek warfare.
Theopompus was a Spartan king; Euphaes was king of the Messenians.
Raising a trophy marked victory, and asking for a truce to bury the dead was the usual way of conceding the field.

literary_notes.text: The Messenians are shown as driven by desperation and patriotism, contrasting with the Spartans' trained steadiness.
Those hoping to profit from the dead meet death themselves, a grim reversal of their intent.
Euphaes uses the Theban myth to frame the battle as a kin-murdering tragedy, taunting the Spartan king.
The claim that the battle seemed only just begun stresses renewed energy when the kings meet.
